questions.stem:
An agent will change the authentication flow of a production service in a GitHub repository named Repo1. The change is difficult to reverse.

You need to ensure that the reviewers agree on the intent of the change before any code is generated. Which workflow should you use?

options.text: A plan-first workflow, in which the agent opens a pull request that contains only the plan
options.rationale: Correct. People validate the intent before any code is written, which is the approach for high-risk changes that are difficult to reverse.

options.text: A plan and execution workflow, in which the plan and the first commits are in the same pull request
options.rationale: Incorrect. Code is generated at once, so the intent is validated only together with the changes. That suits low-risk, reversible work.

options.text: A workflow in which the agent pushes to `main` and records the plan in the commit message
options.rationale: Incorrect. A direct push skips the pull request, which is where the plan and the change are reviewed.

options.text: A workflow in which the agent implements the change and a reviewer writes the plan afterwards
options.rationale: Incorrect. A plan written after the change can't be used to validate intent before the change.

questions.explanation: Both workflows are reviewed before merge. They differ in when a person validates the work relative to the code. Plan-first puts that validation before any code exists, which reduces early exposure for high-risk work such as authentication, infrastructure, workflows and production.
questions.takeaway: High risk or hard to reverse → plan-first. Low risk and reversible → plan and execution.

evidence.quote: The agent opens a pull request that contains only the plan (no code changes yet).
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M2, unit 4

evidence.quote: Use plan-first for high-risk work (workflows, infra, auth, production).
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M2, unit 4

evidence.quote: changes are high-risk or difficult to reverse
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M2, unit 4

whyExam.skill: Configure agent planning to be distinct from agent execution

clues.text: M2 unit 4 gives explicit decision guidance: plan-first for high-risk work (workflows, infra, auth, production).
Plan-first versus plan + execution is the central choice of the unit and returns in M6 (risk-based autonomy).
Both options are reviewed before merge; only the timing of validation differs, which makes an easy distractor.

questions.stem:
You are building a GitHub Actions workflow named `multi-agent-orchestration`. Two analysis agents run in parallel, and a third job merges their outputs into one plan.

You need to ensure that the `plan_merger` job starts only after both analysis jobs finish, and that `plan_merger` jobs for the same branch never run at the same time.

How should you complete the workflow?
questions.template:
jobs:
  spec_analyzer:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: ./executors/spec_analyzer.sh

  risk_reviewer:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: ./executors/risk_reviewer.sh

  plan_merger:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    [[key1]]: [spec_analyzer, risk_reviewer]
    [[key2]]:
      group: multiagent-${{ github.ref }}
    steps:
      - run: ./executors/plan_merger.sh

key1.rationale: `needs` lists the jobs that must complete first, so `plan_merger` waits for both analysis jobs. That is the fan-in. `uses` calls a reusable workflow, `with` passes inputs and `environment` names a deployment environment.

key2.rationale: A `concurrency` group allows only one job in the group to run at a time. Because the group name contains the branch ref, merge jobs for the same branch can't overlap. `strategy` only creates variations of a job inside one run.

questions.explanation: The two analysis jobs have no dependency on each other, so they start in parallel: that is the fan-out. `needs: [spec_analyzer, risk_reviewer]` makes `plan_merger` wait for both: that is the fan-in. A `concurrency` group on the job then keeps two merge jobs for the same branch from running together.
questions.takeaway: Fan-in = `needs` with a list of jobs. No overlap = `concurrency` with a group name.

evidence.quote: To coordinate multiple agents in parallel and then merge their outputs, use the fan-out/fan-in orchestration with needs.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M4, unit 3

evidence.quote: You can also limit the concurrency of jobs within a workflow by using the `concurrency` keyword at the job level:
evidence.label: GitHub Docs

whyExam.skill: Apply an orchestration pattern to coordinate multiple agents

clues.text: M4 unit 3 says of fan-out/fan-in with `needs`: "This pattern is tested in the exam". The strongest clue in the material.
The unit gives the full YAML.
A candidate who passed the live exam (Aug 2026) reported this topic: completing workflow YAML.

questions.stem:
An agent is assigned an issue to remediate a security alert for a vulnerable dependency in a GitHub repository named Repo1. The agent opens a pull request, all required checks pass, and the agent reports that the task is complete. The alert is still open, because the vulnerable version remains reachable through a transitive dependency.

You need to change the task definition so that this outcome is no longer accepted as complete. What should you do?

options.text: Add a second approving review to the ruleset for `main`.
options.rationale: Incorrect. A second reviewer sees the same green checks. Nothing in the task says that the alert must close.

options.text: Instruct the agent to state its confidence level in the pull request description.
options.rationale: Incorrect. Evaluation must rest on system signals, not on how confident the agent is.

options.text: Increase the number of times that the agent may retry failed checks.
options.rationale: Incorrect. No check failed. The checks passed while the real goal was missed.

options.text: Add a success criterion that the alert is resolved, and verify it from the security signal.
options.rationale: Correct. The criterion now states the real intent, and it is verified by a signal that the agent doesn't control.

questions.explanation: The task was judged by "tests passed" when its intent was "vulnerability resolved". Passing checks are necessary, but they only validate what they were built to detect. A success criterion must describe the real outcome and be measured by a system signal, here the state of the alert.
questions.takeaway: Write success criteria for the real intent, and measure them with a system signal.

evidence.quote: "CI passed" is necessary, but not always sufficient. Make success criteria reflect the real intent of the task (for example, "vulnerability resolved" rather than "tests passed").
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M2, unit 3

evidence.quote: These capabilities reinforce a key lesson: agent evaluation must be grounded in system signals, not in the agent's confidence.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M1, unit 3

whyExam.skill: Align evaluation criteria with development intent

clues.text: M2 unit 3 tip: "CI passed is necessary, but not always sufficient."
M1 u.3 and u.5 repeat that evaluation rests on system signals, not on the agent's confidence.

questions.stem:
You are assigning an autonomy level to each agent in a GitHub organization named Org1.

Which autonomy level describes each agent?

targets.text: An agent that runs pre-approved test, build, and staging deployment workflows within defined limits
targets.rationale: It executes, but only workflows that were approved in advance and within limits.

targets.text: An agent that classifies new issues and recommends labels, and that cannot modify anything
targets.rationale: It inspects, classifies and recommends. It changes nothing.

targets.text: An agent that deploys to production only after a reviewer approves the deployment
targets.rationale: A high-impact action happens only after a human approves it.

targets.text: An agent that creates branches and pull requests, and that cannot merge or deploy
targets.rationale: It proposes changes through pull requests. Acceptance stays with people and policy.

questions.explanation: The four levels grow with the impact of what the agent may do: inspect only, propose through pull requests, run pre-approved workflows inside limits, and perform high-impact actions only after a human approves. Autonomy is usually a combination of pull request rules, environments, workflow permissions and tool access, not one setting.
questions.takeaway: Read-only → propose-only → execute with guardrails → human-authorized execution.

evidence.quote: Read-only autonomy: Agent can inspect, summarize, classify, and recommend changes, but can't modify anything.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M6, unit 2

evidence.quote: Propose-only autonomy: Agent can create branches and pull requests, but can't merge or deploy.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M6, unit 2

evidence.quote: Execute with guardrails: Agent can run pre-approved workflows (tests, builds, staging deploys) within defined limits.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M6, unit 2

evidence.quote: Human-authorized execution: Agent can perform high-impact actions only after a human approves (production deploy, workflow changes, secret access).
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M6, unit 2

whyExam.skill: Assign autonomy levels to maximize delivery speed while remaining compliant with organizational security and Responsible AI standards

clues.text: Autonomy levels are a named skill group.
M6 unit 2 defines four named levels, a ready-made matching item.

questions.stem:
An agent works on tasks in a GitHub repository named Repo1 from an IDE, from the CLI, and in a GitHub-hosted environment. You are defining a single source of truth for each type of information.

Where should you store each type of information?

targets.text: The validation rules that apply to every task in the repository
targets.rationale: Rules that hold for every task belong in repository instructions, not in one issue or pull request.

targets.text: The requirements that define a task before any work starts
targets.rationale: Requirements live in the issue, which exists before a branch or pull request does.

targets.text: The results of the tests that validated a change
targets.rationale: Execution results are produced and kept by workflow runs and their artifacts.

targets.text: The decisions taken and the progress made while implementing a task
targets.rationale: The pull request gathers commits, checks and discussion, so decisions and progress are recorded there.

questions.explanation: Each type of information gets one location, so every tool reads the same value. Requirements go in the issue, decisions and progress in the pull request, validation rules in repository instructions, and results in workflow runs and artifacts.
questions.takeaway: Issue = requirements. Pull request = decisions and progress. Instructions = rules. Runs = results.

evidence.quote: Requirements live in issues
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M5, unit 4

evidence.quote: Decisions and progress live in pull requests
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M5, unit 4

evidence.quote: Validation rules live in repository instructions
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M5, unit 4

evidence.quote: Execution results live in workflow runs and artifacts
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M5, unit 4

whyExam.skill: Prevent conflicting context

clues.text: M5 units 2 and 4 both give the same mapping list: requirements → issue, decisions → PR, rules → instructions, results → runs.
The study guide has a skill group for memory and state continuity.

questions.stem:
GitHub Copilot cloud agent works on a .NET repository named Repo1. In each session, the agent spends several minutes discovering and installing the .NET SDK and restoring NuGet packages, and the installation sometimes fails.

You need to preinstall the tools and the dependencies in the agent's environment before the agent starts working. What should you do?

options.text: Add the installation commands to the custom instructions file of the repository.
options.rationale: Incorrect. Instructions tell the agent what to run. The agent would still install everything itself during the session, by trial and error.

options.text: Add a `preToolUse` hook that installs the SDK and the packages before each tool call.
options.rationale: Incorrect. A `preToolUse` hook approves or denies a tool call. It isn't the place to build the environment.

options.text: Add a `copilot-setup-steps.yml` workflow file that installs them, and commit it to the default branch.
options.rationale: Correct. The steps of its `copilot-setup-steps` job run in the agent's environment before the agent starts, so the SDK and the packages are already there.

options.text: Create a workflow that runs on `push` and caches the NuGet packages for later runs.
options.rationale: Incorrect. That workflow runs in its own runner for its own event. It doesn't prepare the environment of an agent session.

questions.explanation: The cloud agent works in an ephemeral environment that is powered by GitHub Actions. You prepare that environment with a workflow file at a fixed path that contains a single job with a fixed name, `copilot-setup-steps`. The file must exist on the default branch.
questions.takeaway: Prepare the agent's environment with `copilot-setup-steps.yml`: fixed path, fixed job name, default branch.

evidence.quote: On GitHub, Copilot in the cloud works in a GitHub Actions-powered environment, creates changes on a branch, and prepares those changes for review.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M3, unit 5

evidence.note: You customize Copilot's environment with a workflow file located at `.github/workflows/copilot-setup-steps.yml`. It must contain a single `copilot-setup-steps` job, whose steps run before Copilot starts working, and it won't trigger unless it is present on the default branch.
evidence.label: GitHub Docs

whyExam.skill: Configure an agent to handle environment-specific constraints

clues.text: The audience profile names "Copilot setup steps" explicitly.
Fixed file path and fixed job name: an unambiguous detail.

questions.stem:
You configure a planning agent. The agent's instructions contain the following text: "Do not edit files. Produce a plan only." During a planning session, the agent modifies two source files.

You need to guarantee that the planning agent cannot modify files. What should you do?

options.text: Repeat the instruction at the start and at the end of the agent's instructions.
options.rationale: Incorrect. An instruction is still guidance, however often it is repeated. The model can fail to follow it.

options.text: Add a required Plan section to the pull request template.
options.rationale: Incorrect. A template makes the plan visible. It doesn't take away the agent's ability to edit files.

options.text: Ask the reviewers to reject every plan that is delivered together with code changes.
options.rationale: Incorrect. That detects the edit after it happened and depends on people noticing it.

options.text: Limit the planning agent to read-only tools.
options.rationale: Correct. Without a tool that can write, the agent has no way to modify a file, whatever it decides to do.

questions.explanation: This is the difference between guidance and enforcement. An instruction asks the agent to behave in a certain way. A capability boundary removes the ability: a planning agent that only has read-only tools cannot change files.
questions.takeaway: Instructions are guidance. Tool allowlists and gates are enforcement.

evidence.quote: A planning agent should be limited to read-only tools so it cannot modify files during planning.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M2, unit 4

evidence.quote: Treat "instructions not to edit" as guidance; treat tool allowlists and gates as enforcement.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M2, unit 4

whyExam.skill: Prevent agent action until the agent checked and approved

clues.text: M2 unit 4: "Treat instructions not to edit as guidance; treat tool allowlists and gates as enforcement."
Guidance versus enforcement recurs in M2 u.7 (hooks), M3 (tools) and M6 u.3 ("controls in docs only").
Instructions look like a control. Exams like options that only ask the model to behave.

questions.stem:
You have a GitHub repository named Repo1 that contains two workflow files. The first workflow is named `CI Validation` and builds and tests pull requests from a dependency agent. The second workflow is named `Security Validation`.

You need to ensure that Security Validation starts automatically each time a CI Validation run finishes. You must not change the CI Validation workflow file.

Which trigger event should you configure in Security Validation?

options.text: `workflow_dispatch`
options.rationale: Incorrect. `workflow_dispatch` starts a run manually or through the API. Nothing would start it when CI Validation finishes.

options.text: `workflow_run`
options.rationale: Correct. `workflow_run` names the `CI Validation` workflow and reacts to its `completed` activity type, without any change to that workflow.

options.text: `workflow_call`
options.rationale: Incorrect. `workflow_call` makes Security Validation reusable, but CI Validation would then have to call it, and you must not change that file.

options.text: `pull_request`
options.rationale: Incorrect. Both workflows would start together on each push to the pull request, so Security Validation wouldn't wait for CI to finish.

questions.explanation: Sequential orchestration means one step runs only after another has finished. Between two separate workflows, the `workflow_run` trigger expresses that order: the second workflow names the first one and reacts to its `completed` activity type.
questions.takeaway: Run workflow B after workflow A, without touching A: `on: workflow_run` in B.

evidence.quote: workflow completion triggers when one step should run after another.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M4, unit 3

evidence.quote: Use this pattern when one agent's output must be validated before another step can proceed.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M4, unit 3

evidence.quote: This event occurs when a workflow run is requested or completed. It allows you to execute a workflow based on execution or completion of another workflow.
evidence.label: GitHub Docs

whyExam.skill: Apply an orchestration pattern to coordinate multiple agents

clues.text: M4 unit 3 shows the `workflow_run` YAML for sequential orchestration.
`workflow_call` and `workflow_dispatch` are close distractors.

questions.stem:
You are analyzing four failed agent tasks in a GitHub repository named Repo1 so that you can decide what to improve.

Which root cause category does each failure belong to?

targets.text: The agent based its change on a pull request state that newer commits had replaced.
targets.rationale: The agent worked from stale information: an outdated pull request state.

targets.text: The agent implemented a discount rule that ignores one of the acceptance criteria in the issue.
targets.rationale: The information was available and correct. The agent's decision was wrong.

targets.text: The validation never ran, because the agent's workflow was configured for the wrong event.
targets.rationale: A workflow was misconfigured and wasn't triggered properly.

targets.text: The issue and the pull request description gave different values for a timeout, and the agent applied the wrong one.
targets.rationale: Two artifacts held conflicting information, so the context itself was faulty.

questions.explanation: The category points to the fix. A reasoning error is fixed with clearer prompts and instructions. Tool misuse is fixed in the tool configuration, such as workflow triggers and permissions. A context issue is fixed in memory and state: remove stale or conflicting information and keep one source of truth.
questions.takeaway: Wrong decision = reasoning. Wrong use of a workflow or command = tool. Stale, missing or conflicting information = context.

evidence.quote: Ignoring acceptance criteria
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M5, unit 6

evidence.quote: Failing to trigger or use workflows properly
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M5, unit 6

evidence.quote: Using outdated pull request state
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M5, unit 6

evidence.quote: Conflicting information across artifacts
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M5, unit 6

whyExam.skill: Classify root causes, including reasoning errors, tool misuse, and context or environment issues

clues.text: The bullet names the three categories used in M5 unit 6.
The unit gives examples per category, ready-made matching items.

questions.stem:
A workflow named `agent-plan-apply` has a job named `plan` that reads a machine-readable risk rating from an agent's plan and exposes it as the job output `risk`.

Plans that are rated `low` must be applied automatically. All other plans must wait for the approval of the required reviewers of an environment named `approval-required`.

You need to route each plan according to its risk rating.

How should you complete the workflow?
questions.template:
apply:
    needs: plan
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    [[gate]]: approval-required
    if: ${{ needs.plan.outputs.risk [[apply_if]] 'low' }}
    steps:
      - run: ./scripts/apply.sh out/plan.json

  apply_auto:
    needs: plan
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    if: ${{ needs.plan.outputs.risk [[auto_if]] 'low' }}
    steps:
      - run: ./scripts/apply.sh out/plan.json

gate.rationale: A job that references an environment with required reviewers waits until a reviewer approves it. `concurrency` only serializes runs, and `permissions` only scopes the token.

apply_if.rationale: The gated job must run for every rating that is not `low`.

auto_if.rationale: The job without a gate must run only when the rating is `low`.

questions.explanation: The risk rating is a job output, so the routing is decided by the workflow and not by a description that someone has to interpret. The job for anything other than `low` targets the environment and therefore waits for approval. The job for `low` has no environment and runs at once.
questions.takeaway: Route on a machine-readable risk signal: `if` picks the job, `environment` adds the approval.

evidence.quote: Decision guidance: Don’t rely on narrative explanations of risk. Use a machine-readable signal and enforce routing.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M6, unit 2

evidence.quote: High-risk plans require explicit human approval
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M6, unit 2

evidence.quote: Jobs that reference an environment configured with required reviewers will wait for an approval before starting.
evidence.label: GitHub Docs

whyExam.skill: Classify agent actions by operational, security, and compliance risk to right-size human interventions

clues.text: M6 unit 2: "Don't rely on narrative explanations of risk. Use a machine-readable signal and enforce routing."
The unit gives the complete YAML with `needs.plan.outputs.risk` and `environment`.

questions.stem:
An agent started work on an issue in a GitHub repository named Repo1 and opened a pull request. The session ended before the work was complete. A new agent session must now finish the task.

You need to ensure that the new session continues the work without repeating completed steps. What should the agent do first?

options.text: Create a new branch from `main` and implement the issue again from its description.
options.rationale: Incorrect. This discards the commits already made and repeats the work.

options.text: Ask the user to paste the chat history of the earlier session into the prompt.
options.rationale: Incorrect. Chat history is session context. It may be incomplete, and it isn't the recorded state of the work.

options.text: Open the existing pull request and review its description, linked issue, commits, and check results.
options.rationale: Correct. The pull request holds the plan, the work done and the validation results, so the agent can continue from the latest state.

options.text: Close the pull request and open a new one that references the same issue.
options.rationale: Incorrect. Recreating the pull request is a reset, used when requirements or the approach change. Nothing changed here.

questions.explanation: State is stored in GitHub artifacts, not in the session. To resume, the agent opens the existing pull request, reads the description and linked issue, checks the commits and the results in the Checks tab, and continues from there.
questions.takeaway: To resume, re-anchor to the pull request, never to the previous session.

evidence.quote: Agent workflows may pause or move between environments. To resume work correctly, the agent should rely on stored state instead of starting over.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M5, unit 3

evidence.quote: Because GitHub preserves commit history and workflow runs, the agent can identify completed work and avoid duplication.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M5, unit 3

whyExam.skill: Resume agent work without repeating steps or diverging from prior decisions

clues.text: The study-guide bullet matches the unit's resume flow almost word for word.
M5 unit 3 gives a numbered resume flow.

questions.stem:
You are adding a remote MCP server for a ticketing system to the MCP configuration of GitHub Copilot cloud agent for a GitHub repository named Repo1. The agent must be able to use only the tools named `get_ticket` and `search_tickets`.

You need to configure the MCP server for the agent.

How should you complete the configuration?

root.rationale: The cloud agent's configuration is a JSON object with an `mcpServers` object, in which each key is a server name. `servers` is the root key of the VS Code configuration file.

type.rationale: A remote server is reached over the network. `local` and `stdio` start a process from a `command` with `args`.

endpoint.rationale: A remote server requires `url`. `command` and `args` are the required keys of a local server.

questions.explanation: An MCP server exposes tools, and the configuration decides which of them the agent gets. For the cloud agent, every server needs `type` and `tools`. A remote server also needs `url`, and a local one needs `command` and `args`. Listing the two read-only tools, and not `*`, keeps the agent's reach narrow, which matters because the agent uses configured tools without asking for approval.
questions.takeaway: Cloud agent MCP: `mcpServers` → server → `type`, `tools`, and `url` or `command` with `args`.

evidence.quote: Namespace control: prefer enabling a narrow tool subset rather than broad wildcards.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M2, unit 7

evidence.quote: A remote MCP server is hosted elsewhere and accessed over the network.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M3, unit 3

evidence.quote: The JSON must contain an `mcpServers` object, where the key is the name of the MCP server (for example, `sentry`), and the value is an object with the configuration for that MCP server.
evidence.label: GitHub Docs

whyExam.skill: Add an MCP server as a tool to an agent

clues.text: Four study-guide bullets are about MCP servers.
JSON configuration with `type`, `url` and `tools`: a natural drop-down item.
A candidate who passed the live exam (Aug 2026) reported this topic: restricting the tools of an MCP server.
`servers` (VS Code) versus `mcpServers` (cloud agent).

questions.stem:
You are describing how GitHub acts as the control plane for the work of agents.

For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

items.statement: CODEOWNERS routes review requests based on the paths that a pull request changes.
items.explanation: CODEOWNERS maps paths to owners, and the owners are requested as reviewers when those paths change.

items.statement: A job that targets an environment with required reviewers starts immediately and requests approval after it finishes.
items.explanation: The job waits. It starts only after a required reviewer approves, which is what protects the environment's secrets.

items.statement: Required status checks turn evaluation into a policy that is enforced before merging.
items.explanation: A required check must pass before the merge, so the evidence from CI becomes a condition and not just information.

questions.explanation: GitHub is the control plane because it has enforcement points that shape what an agent's contribution can do: pull requests, required reviews, required status checks, CODEOWNERS, rulesets and environments. Each one enforces something specific, and each has to be turned on.
questions.takeaway: CODEOWNERS routes, required checks enforce evidence, environments hold a job until approval.

evidence.quote: If a workflow job targets an environment with required reviewers, the job waits until approval is granted.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M1, unit 4

evidence.quote: The supervision model works everywhere; enforcement requires the controls to be turned on.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M1, unit 4

evidence.quote: Jobs that reference an environment configured with required reviewers will wait for an approval before starting.
evidence.label: GitHub Docs

whyExam.skill: Plan and implement the degree of agent autonomy, including guardrails

clues.text: M1 unit 4 has a "Controls at a glance" table: each GitHub control and what it enforces.
The audience profile describes GitHub as "the system of record and control plane".
Environment reviewers act before the job starts, not after.

questions.stem:
A GitHub repository named Repo1 has two workflows named `agent-lint` and `agent-tests`. Both run on every push to a pull request branch, and several agent sessions push to the same branches many times an hour. Both workflows contain the following block.

```yaml
concurrency:
  group: ${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true
```

You discover that an `agent-tests` run is canceled whenever `agent-lint` starts on the same branch.

You need to ensure that each workflow cancels only its own outdated runs on a branch. What should you do?

options.text: Set `cancel-in-progress` to `false` in both workflows.
options.rationale: Incorrect. Both workflows would still share one group per branch, so the runs of one workflow would wait for, or replace pending runs of, the other.

options.text: Move the `concurrency` block from the workflow level to each job.
options.rationale: Incorrect. The group name would still be the branch ref alone, so the jobs of both workflows would stay in the same group.

options.text: Change the group to `${{ github.run_id }}` in both workflows.
options.rationale: Incorrect. A run ID is unique, so every run would be alone in its group and outdated runs would never be canceled.

options.text: Change the group to `${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}` in both workflows.
options.rationale: Correct. The group is now specific to one workflow on one branch, so a new run cancels only the earlier run of the same workflow.

questions.explanation: A concurrency group belongs to the repository, not to a workflow. With `${{ github.ref }}` alone, every workflow that uses that group shares one slot per branch, so `agent-lint` cancels `agent-tests`. Adding `${{ github.workflow }}` to the name gives each workflow its own group on each branch.
questions.takeaway: Group names must be unique across workflows: `${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}`.

evidence.quote: Setting only `${{ github.ref }}` without workflow makes concurrency global to the branch, potentially blocking unrelated workflows from running.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M4, unit 4

evidence.quote: If you have multiple workflows in the same repository, concurrency group names must be unique across workflows to avoid canceling in-progress jobs or runs from other workflows.
evidence.label: GitHub Docs

whyExam.skill: Configure agent isolation for parallel execution

clues.text: M4 unit 4 has a dedicated section and a Note on the group name; M6 u.4 reuses concurrency.
Docs: group names must be unique across workflows.
`${{ github.ref }}` alone, matrix, and job-level concurrency are all offered as alternatives in the unit.

questions.stem:
An agent in a GitHub repository named Repo1 often produces pull requests that fail validation. You run the agent on a task, and you need to improve its behavior by using a feedback loop.

Which four actions should you perform in sequence after the agent has run?

items.text: Observe the failures in the workflow logs and artifacts.
Identify the root cause of the failures.
Apply a fix to the prompts, the memory, or the tool configuration.
Remove the failing checks from the required status checks.
Grant write access for all scopes to the workflow token.

questions.explanation: Improvement is iterative: look at the evidence first, name the cause, change the one thing that the cause points to, and run again to confirm. Removing checks or widening permissions hides the failure instead of correcting the behavior.
questions.takeaway: Observe → root cause → fix prompts, memory or tools → re-run.

evidence.quote: Observe failures through logs and artifacts
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M5, unit 6

evidence.quote: Identify the root cause
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M5, unit 6

evidence.quote: Apply fixes to prompts, memory, or tools
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M5, unit 6

evidence.quote: Re-run the workflow
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M5, unit 6

whyExam.skill: Revise instructions, workflows, or constraints

clues.text: M5 unit 6 gives the feedback loop as numbered steps: a build-list item.
Removing checks or widening permissions are tempting "fixes".

questions.stem:
An agent opens a pull request in a GitHub repository named Repo1. A required code scanning check fails, because the change introduces a vulnerability. The agent pushes three more commits that rearrange the code, and the check fails each time with the same alert. The team's recovery policy allows bounded retries for transient failures.

You need to apply the correct recovery strategy. What should occur next?

options.text: The agent continues to push new commits until the check passes.
options.rationale: Incorrect. The failure isn't transient, and repeated attempts with the same result are a loop that the policy is meant to stop.

options.text: The check is removed from the required status checks for pull requests that agents open.
options.rationale: Incorrect. That removes the control that detected the problem and creates a bypass path.

options.text: Automated iteration stops, and the failure is escalated to a human for investigation.
options.rationale: Correct. A security failure is investigated, not retried, and a failure that repeats with the same signature is escalated.

options.text: The agent dismisses the alert as a false positive and requests a review.
options.rationale: Incorrect. The agent would be deciding on its own evidence. A person must judge a security finding.

questions.explanation: Recovery strategies depend on the kind of failure. A transient failure, such as a network error, may be retried within a limit. A security failure isn't transient: it is investigated. And when the same required check fails repeatedly with the same signature, automation stops and a human takes over.
questions.takeaway: Retry transient failures. Investigate security failures. Escalate repeated ones.

evidence.quote: Investigate security failures instead of repeatedly retrying
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M6, unit 7

evidence.quote: Escalate after repeated failures
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M6, unit 7

evidence.quote: if required checks fail twice with the same failure signature, or
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M4, unit 5

whyExam.skill: Require explicit authorization or controlled paths for irreversible or compliance-sensitive changes

clues.text: M6 unit 7: "Investigate security failures instead of repeatedly retrying".
"Escalate after the same failure twice" appears in M2 u.7, M4 u.5 and u.7.

questions.stem:
An agent is implementing an issue in a GitHub repository named Repo1. The acceptance criteria require input validation for one API endpoint. After several iterations, the pull request also contains a refactoring of the logging subsystem, and the latest commits contradict a design decision that is recorded in the pull request description.

You need to correct the context drift. What should the agent do first?

options.text: Re-read the issue and the pull request, and compare the changes with the acceptance criteria.
options.rationale: Correct. Drift is corrected by returning to the source of truth and measuring the changes against it.

options.text: Update the acceptance criteria in the issue so that they include the logging refactoring.
options.rationale: Incorrect. That changes the goal to match the drift. The requirement didn't change.

options.text: Start a new session that continues from the agent's own summary of its earlier work.
options.rationale: Incorrect. The agent's summary carries the same drifted context forward.

options.text: Merge the pull request and create a follow-up issue for the logging changes.
options.rationale: Incorrect. That accepts changes that don't match the acceptance criteria.

questions.explanation: Two signs of drift appear here: changes that go beyond the acceptance criteria and commits that contradict an earlier decision. The correction starts by re-reading the issue and the pull request description, then comparing the changes with the criteria.
questions.takeaway: Drift is corrected against the source of truth, not against the agent's own account.

evidence.quote: Context drift occurs when the agent’s actions no longer align with the original goal or prior decisions.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M5, unit 3

evidence.quote: To correct drift, the agent should be re-aligned with the source of truth.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M5, unit 3

evidence.quote: Compare current changes with acceptance criteria
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M5, unit 3

whyExam.skill: Detect and correct drift during extended agent execution

clues.text: Drift detection and correction is a named skill.
M5 unit 3 lists the signs of drift and the steps to correct it.

questions.stem:
A scheduled workflow in a GitHub repository named Repo1 runs an agent that commits generated documentation to a branch by using the `GITHUB_TOKEN`. A second workflow that runs on `push` and publishes the documentation never starts after these commits.

You need to ensure that the publishing workflow runs after the agent's commits. The solution must not use long-lived personal credentials.

What should you do?

options.text: Grant the `contents: write` permission to the `GITHUB_TOKEN`.
options.rationale: Incorrect. The token can already push. The limit is that events caused by `GITHUB_TOKEN` don't start new workflow runs.

options.text: Push the commits by using an installation access token of a GitHub App.
options.rationale: Correct. A push made with an app token creates the `push` event that starts the workflow, and the token is short-lived and not tied to a person.

options.text: Push the commits by using a personal access token of a repository administrator.
options.rationale: Incorrect. It would trigger the workflow, but it is a long-lived personal credential.

options.text: Change the trigger of the publishing workflow from `push` to `pull_request`.
options.rationale: Incorrect. No pull request is involved, so the workflow would still not start.

questions.explanation: Events that are triggered with the repository's `GITHUB_TOKEN` don't create new workflow runs, which protects against recursive runs. To start one workflow from another on purpose, use a different credential. A GitHub App installation token does that without a personal credential, and the design must then avoid loops.
questions.takeaway: `GITHUB_TOKEN` pushes don't trigger workflows. Use a GitHub App token when one must.

evidence.quote: Most actions performed with this token don't trigger extra workflow runs, which helps prevent unintended loops or repeated execution.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M3, unit 5

evidence.quote: Other authentication methods, such as GitHub App tokens or personal access tokens (PATs), can trigger extra workflow runs depending on configuration.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M3, unit 5

evidence.quote: For example, if a workflow run pushes code using the repository's `GITHUB_TOKEN`, a new workflow will not run even when the repository contains a workflow configured to run when `push` events occur.
evidence.label: GitHub Docs

whyExam.skill: Configure agent tool permissions

clues.text: M3 unit 5 has a section on trigger behaviour of `GITHUB_TOKEN` versus App tokens and PATs.
A candidate who passed the live exam (Aug 2026) reported this topic: `GITHUB_TOKEN` scope and permissions blocks.
Adding `contents: write` doesn't help, a common wrong fix.

questions.stem:
You are building a workflow in which a job named `plan` generates a plan and a job named `implement` uses it.

You need to pass the plan from the `plan` job to the `implement` job as a job output.

How should you complete the workflow?
questions.template:
jobs:
  plan:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    outputs:
      plan: ${{ steps.generate_plan.outputs.plan }}
    steps:
      - id: generate_plan
        run: echo "plan=..." >> "[[file]]"

  implement:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    [[dep]]: plan
    steps:
      - run: echo "Using plan: ${{ [[expr]] }}"

file.rationale: A step sets an output by writing `name=value` to `$GITHUB_OUTPUT`. `$GITHUB_ENV` sets an environment variable for later steps of the same job, and `$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY` writes the run summary.

dep.rationale: `needs` makes `implement` depend on `plan`, which orders the jobs and gives access to the outputs of `plan`.

expr.rationale: A dependent job reads a job output through the `needs` context. The `steps` context only reaches steps of the same job.

questions.explanation: Data moves through a workflow in two stages. A step writes an output to `$GITHUB_OUTPUT`, and the job publishes it under `outputs`. Another job declares `needs` and reads the value from `needs.<job>.outputs.<name>`. Environment variables configure a job and aren't a substitute for this.
questions.takeaway: Step output → job `outputs` → `needs.<job>.outputs.<name>` in the dependent job.

evidence.quote: Step outputs pass values between steps in the same job.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M2, unit 6

evidence.quote: Job outputs pass values across jobs (through job dependencies).
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M2, unit 6

evidence.quote: Environment variables configure runtime behavior but shouldn't replace outputs for structured data flow.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M2, unit 6

whyExam.skill: Configure an agent to be invoked in a CI workflow

clues.text: M2 unit 6 shows step outputs, job outputs and `needs` in YAML, a natural code-completion item.
The unit stresses "Outputs are workflow contracts" and contrasts them with `env`.
A candidate who passed the live exam (Aug 2026) reported this topic: completing workflow YAML.

questions.stem:
Several agents work in a GitHub repository named Repo1, and you are classifying the conflicts that occurred last month.

Which conflict type does each situation describe?

targets.text: Two pull requests merge cleanly, but the combined build fails because one renamed a method that the other calls.
targets.rationale: The merge is clean and the combined behavior is broken.

targets.text: Two agents open separate pull requests that fix the same code scanning alert in different ways.
targets.rationale: Two pull requests solve the same problem differently.

targets.text: Two agents change the same lines of the same file in separate pull requests.
targets.rationale: The same files and lines were changed.

targets.text: One pull request changes application code and a workflow file, and the two areas require approval from different teams.
targets.rationale: Protected areas require different reviews or approvals.

questions.explanation: Naming the type tells you which control detects it. A textual conflict is visible in the pull request. A semantic conflict is only caught by checks that build and test the combined result. A policy conflict is resolved by ownership routing, and duplicate effort by clear responsibilities for each agent.
questions.takeaway: Clean merge but broken result = semantic conflict. Only checks catch it.

evidence.quote: Textual merge conflicts (same files/lines changed).
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M4, unit 5

evidence.quote: Semantic conflicts (clean merge, broken combined behavior).
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M4, unit 5

evidence.quote: Policy conflicts (protected areas require different reviews/approvals).
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M4, unit 5

evidence.quote: Duplicate effort (two PRs solving the same problem differently).
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M4, unit 5

whyExam.skill: Detect and resolve agent conflicts, including overlapping code changes, duplicated effort, and contradictory outputs

clues.text: The bullet names the conflict types almost exactly.
M4 unit 5 lists four types, a ready-made matching item.

questions.scenario:
You have a GitHub repository named Repo1. The `main` branch has no rulesets and no branch protection rules. Agents open pull requests that target `main`. A workflow named `ci.yml` runs for every pull request that targets `main` and reports a check named `test`.

You need to ensure that a pull request cannot be merged into `main` unless the tests pass.

items.solution: You create an active ruleset that targets `main` and requires a pull request with one approving review before merging.
items.explanation: A reviewer can approve while `test` is failing. Nothing requires the check to pass.

items.solution: You create an active ruleset that targets `main`, and you add `test` as a required status check.
items.explanation: The ruleset blocks the merge until `test` passes, whoever opened or approved the pull request.

items.solution: You create a branch protection rule for `main`, select **Require status checks to pass before merging**, and select the `test` check.
items.explanation: A branch protection rule with `test` selected as a required status check enforces the same gate as the ruleset.

questions.explanation: A check that runs is only information. It becomes a gate when it is selected as a required status check, in a ruleset or in a branch protection rule. Required reviews are a separate control: they gate on human approval, not on test results.
questions.takeaway: Tests gate a merge only as a required status check. Rulesets and branch protection can both do it.

evidence.quote: Required checks ensure that certain conditions must be met before a pull request can be merged.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M5, unit 5

evidence.quote: When this workflow is configured as a required check (via rulesets or branch protection), a pull request can't be merged until the check passes.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M2, unit 3

whyExam.skill: Specify expected outcomes and operational constraints for agent tasks

clues.text: Required status checks appear in nearly every module.
M2 unit 3: "success is enforced by the system, not assumed by the agent".

questions.stem:
In a GitHub organization named Org1, agents open about 60 pull requests each day. An audit shows that reviewers approve most of them in less than a minute, without opening the changes. The pull requests are large, and they contain no test or scan results.

You need to restore meaningful review without adding more approval steps. What should you do?

options.text: Require three approving reviews instead of one for every pull request.
options.rationale: Incorrect. More approvals of the same kind add friction and fatigue. Three quick clicks aren't a review.

options.text: Add the reviewers to the bypass list of the ruleset so that merging is faster.
options.rationale: Incorrect. A bypass list is a way around the policy, which is the opposite of oversight.

options.text: Allow the agents to merge their own pull requests when all checks pass.
options.rationale: Incorrect. That removes human judgment instead of restoring it.

options.text: Require evidence in pull requests, route reviews by using CODEOWNERS, and keep pull requests small.
options.rationale: Correct. Evidence makes review fast, CODEOWNERS sends each change to people who have the context, and small pull requests can actually be read.

questions.explanation: This is rubber-stamping: approvals have become a click to unblock. The cause is governance fatigue, so the remedy is to make each review easier, not to add reviews. Require evidence such as tests and scans, route reviews through CODEOWNERS, and keep pull requests small and scoped.
questions.takeaway: Rubber-stamping → better evidence, CODEOWNERS routing, smaller pull requests.

evidence.quote: require evidence (tests, scans, artifacts) so review is fast
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M6, unit 4

evidence.quote: route reviews via CODEOWNERS so reviewers have context
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M6, unit 4

evidence.quote: keep PRs small and scoped
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M6, unit 4

whyExam.skill: Preserve execution velocity by minimizing approvals that do not materially reduce risk

clues.text: M6 unit 7 has an anti-pattern table with "Rubber-stamping"; M6 u.4 lists how to avoid governance fatigue.
"Add more approvals" looks safe but is the opposite of the remedy.

questions.stem:
A private GitHub repository named Repo1 has a workflow that uploads test reports as workflow artifacts for an agent's pull requests. The repository uses the default retention setting, and the organization does not limit the retention period.

An auditor requires that every report uploaded from now on is available for 180 days after the run.

You need to meet the requirement. What should you do?

options.text: Take no action. Artifacts are kept until someone deletes them.
options.rationale: Incorrect. By default, artifacts and logs are deleted automatically after 90 days.

options.text: Change the visibility of Repo1 to public, and then set the retention period to 180 days.
options.rationale: Incorrect. A public repository allows a retention period of 1 to 90 days only.

options.text: Add `retention-days: 180` to the upload step and keep the repository setting unchanged.
options.rationale: Incorrect. The value on the step can't exceed the repository's retention limit, which is still 90 days.

options.text: Change the artifact and log retention period of Repo1 to 180 days.
options.rationale: Correct. A private repository accepts a retention period of 1 to 400 days, and the new period applies to artifacts created from now on.

questions.explanation: Workflow artifacts are memory that expires. The default is 90 days. The period can be changed: up to 90 days for public repositories and up to 400 days for private ones. A change applies only to new artifacts, which is what the auditor asks for.
questions.takeaway: Default 90 days. Public: 1 to 90. Private: 1 to 400. Not retroactive.

evidence.quote: Public repositories typically allow 1-90 days, while private repositories can extend retention up to 400 days
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M5, unit 3

evidence.quote: By default, checks, workflow runs, commit statuses, and the artifacts and log files generated by workflows are retained for 90 days before they are automatically deleted.
evidence.label: GitHub Docs

evidence.quote: The `retention-days` value cannot exceed the retention limit set by the repository, organization, or enterprise.
evidence.label: GitHub Docs

whyExam.skill: Define memory expiration, pruning, and reset rules

clues.text: M5 unit 3 puts the retention limits in bold, and unit 5 repeats the 90-day default.
Numbers (90, 1–90, 1–400) are exact and testable.
`retention-days` can't exceed the repository limit.

questions.stem:
GitHub Copilot cloud agent opens a pull request in a GitHub repository named Repo1. The repository uses the default settings for the agent. On the pull request, the CI workflow has not started.

You review the changes and find no problems. You need to run the CI workflow for the pull request. What should you do?

options.text: Ask the agent to push an empty commit to the branch of the pull request.
options.rationale: Incorrect. A new commit from the agent is held back in the same way.

options.text: Close the pull request and reopen it.
options.rationale: Incorrect. Reopening doesn't approve the runs. They still wait for a person.

options.text: Add Copilot as a bypass actor in the ruleset for `main`.
options.rationale: Incorrect. A ruleset bypass concerns branch rules. It has nothing to do with the approval of workflow runs.

options.text: Select **Approve and run workflows** as a user who has write access.
options.rationale: Correct. By default, workflows don't run on the agent's code until a user with write access has reviewed it and approves the runs.

questions.explanation: Workflows can have access to secrets and to a token with write permissions, so code written by an agent is treated as untrusted until a person has looked at it. By default the runs wait for **Approve and run workflows**. The repository can be configured to run them automatically, which is a decision about risk.
questions.takeaway: CI not starting on an agent pull request → a user with write access must approve the runs.

evidence.quote: In some agent PR workflows, a human may need to explicitly approve running workflows (for example, an "Approve and run workflows" action). This is a built-in guardrail: it reduces the risk of privileged workflows running automatically for untrusted changes.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M1, unit 4

evidence.note: By default, workflows are not triggered until Copilot cloud agent's code is reviewed and a user with write access to the repository clicks the **Approve and run workflows** button. Optionally, you can configure Copilot to allow workflows to run automatically.
evidence.label: GitHub Docs

whyExam.skill: Enable an agent to perform autonomous actions, including creating branches and pull requests

clues.text: M1 unit 4 presents "Approve and run workflows" as a built-in guardrail; M2 u.5 repeats it.
Docs describe the default precisely, including who can approve.

questions.stem:
You are defining a risk-based autonomy model for an agent in a GitHub repository named Repo1. One class of tasks changes production deployment settings and uses production secrets.

You need to ensure that the agent cannot run the deployment itself, and that the production secrets are released to a job only after a person approves.

Which autonomy design should you apply to this class of tasks?

options.text: Automatic merge after the required checks pass
options.rationale: Incorrect. That is the design for low-risk work such as documentation and formatting.

options.text: A pull request with required checks and at least one review
options.rationale: Incorrect. That is the design for medium-risk work. It gates the merge, not the deployment or the secrets.

options.text: Environment approvals, where the agent prepares the change but cannot execute it
options.rationale: Correct. A job that targets a protected environment waits for approval, and the environment's secrets aren't available before that.

options.text: CODEOWNERS review with multiple reviews and stricter rulesets
options.rationale: Incorrect. That is the design for high-risk paths such as `infra/`. It controls who approves a merge, not access to secrets.

questions.explanation: Autonomy is designed per risk level. Critical work, such as production deployments and secrets, is controlled at the point of execution: the job targets an environment with required reviewers, so it pauses until a person approves, and only then can it read the environment's secrets. The agent prepares the change and can't carry it out.
questions.takeaway: Critical risk → environment approvals: the agent prepares, a person releases.

evidence.quote: If an environment is configured with required reviewers, a job targeting that environment will pause until approval is granted.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M2, unit 6

evidence.quote: This design allows the agent to prepare changes while preventing it from executing production-impacting actions independently.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M2, unit 6

evidence.quote: Secrets stored in an environment are only available to workflow jobs that reference the environment. If the environment requires approval, a job cannot access environment secrets until one of the required reviewers approves it.
evidence.label: GitHub Docs

whyExam.skill: Plan and implement the degree of agent autonomy, including guardrails

clues.text: The risk tiers (low, medium, high, critical) appear in M2 u.6 and again in M6 u.2.
Docs define exactly when environment secrets become available (after approval).
Each tier has a different control; picking the control of the neighbouring tier is the usual mistake.

questions.stem:
A GitHub repository named Repo1 receives pull requests from several agents. Conflicts between the pull requests and the `main` branch are often discovered late, after reviewers have already approved the changes.

You need to ensure that a conflict with `main` is detected automatically each time an agent updates a pull request, and that the result is enforced before merging. The solution must not depend on reviewers noticing the conflict.

What should you do?

options.text: Add a job that runs `git merge --no-commit origin/main`, and make it a required status check.
options.rationale: Correct. The job fails when the branch can't be merged, and as a required check it blocks the merge without anyone having to notice.

options.text: Add a CODEOWNERS entry that assigns all files in the repository to the core team.
options.rationale: Incorrect. CODEOWNERS routes review requests. It doesn't test whether the branch merges with `main`.

options.text: Add `cancel-in-progress: true` to the `concurrency` block of the CI workflow.
options.rationale: Incorrect. That cancels outdated runs. It reports nothing about conflicts.

options.text: Add a section named Conflicts to the pull request template that agents must complete.
options.rationale: Incorrect. A template section is a reminder for people, which is exactly what the solution must not depend on.

questions.explanation: A merge validation step turns a conflict into a failed check as soon as the branch is updated. Making that check required is what makes it enforceable: the pull request can't merge until the check passes, whoever reviews it.
questions.takeaway: Detect conflicts with a check, then make the check required.

evidence.quote: GitHub PRs show merge conflicts, but teams often add a merge validation step so conflicts fail fast as checks:
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M4, unit 5

evidence.quote: If this is a required check, conflicts become enforceable and don’t depend on reviewers noticing them manually.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M4, unit 5

whyExam.skill: Detect and resolve agent conflicts, including overlapping code changes, duplicated effort, and contradictory outputs

clues.text: M4 unit 5 shows the merge validation step.
"If this is a required check, conflicts become enforceable."

questions.stem:
A GitHub repository named Repo1 has a ruleset that requires a status check named `integration-tests` before merging into `main`. The check is reported by a job in a workflow that runs on `pull_request`. To save runner time, a developer adds the following line to the job.

```yaml
if: contains(github.event.pull_request.labels.*.name, 'run-integration')
```

An agent opens a pull request that does not have the label. The job is skipped, and the pull request is merged.

You need to explain why the required check did not block the merge. What is the cause?

options.text: Required status checks are not evaluated for pull requests that agents open.
options.rationale: Incorrect. Required checks apply to every pull request that targets the branch, whoever opens it.

options.text: A required check that is never reported is treated as passed.
options.rationale: Incorrect. A check that isn't reported stays pending, and a pending required check blocks the merge.

options.text: A job that is skipped by a condition reports its status as Success.
options.rationale: Correct. A skipped job counts as successful, so the required check is satisfied without any test having run.

options.text: A ruleset is bypassed when a pull request has no labels.
options.rationale: Incorrect. Labels have no effect on whether a ruleset applies.

questions.explanation: The two cases behave in opposite ways. A job skipped by an `if` condition reports Success and doesn't block the merge, even as a required check. A workflow that is skipped entirely, for example by a path or branch filter, leaves the check pending, and that blocks the merge. An evaluation signal is only as good as the guarantee that it actually ran.
questions.takeaway: Skipped job = Success. Skipped workflow = Pending, which blocks.

evidence.quote: Whether workflow checks are failing or missing
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M5, unit 3

evidence.quote: A job that is skipped will report its status as "Success". It will not prevent a pull request from merging, even if it is a required check.
evidence.label: GitHub Docs

whyExam.skill: Identify failures by using logs, plans, traces, outputs, and workflow artifacts

clues.text: Docs state it bluntly: a skipped job reports Success, even for a required check.
Skipped job (passes) versus skipped workflow (pending, blocks).

questions.stem:
You run GitHub Copilot CLI from a script by using the following command.

```bash
copilot -p "Summarize the last 10 commits and highlight breaking changes."
```

The command has the following requirements:

- Copilot must be able to run `git` commands without asking for approval.
- Copilot must never run `git push`.
- No other tool may be approved automatically.

You need to meet the requirements. Which two options should you add to the command? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

options.text: `--allow-tool='shell(git)'`
options.rationale: Correct. This approves `git` commands only, so every other tool still needs approval.

options.text: `--allow-all-tools`
options.rationale: Incorrect. This approves every tool, including file edits and any shell command.

options.text: `--deny-tool='shell(git push)'`
options.rationale: Correct. A deny rule takes precedence over allow rules, so `git push` is blocked although `git` is allowed.

options.text: `--allow-tool='write'`
options.rationale: Incorrect. This approves tools that modify files, which the task doesn't need.

options.text: `--allow-tool='shell'`
options.rationale: Incorrect. Without a command in parentheses, this approves every shell command.

questions.explanation: For a terminal-based agent, tool access is the governance boundary. Allow exactly what the task needs, here the `git` command, and deny the one subcommand that has consequences. Because `--deny-tool` takes precedence over `--allow-tool`, the two options combine safely.
questions.takeaway: Allow narrowly with `--allow-tool='shell(COMMAND)'`. `--deny-tool` wins over any allow.

evidence.quote: Decision guidance: Match tool access to consequence. Low-risk tasks shouldn't inherit high-risk capabilities.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M6, unit 2

evidence.quote: This pattern helps you support read-only analysis (like commit summarization) without granting broad write capability or auto-approving unrelated tools.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M6, unit 2

evidence.quote: This option takes precedence over the `--allow-all-tools` and `--allow-tool` options.
evidence.label: GitHub Docs

whyExam.skill: Scope permissions and execution contexts to enforce least-privilege access

clues.text: M6 unit 2: "Match tool access to consequence", with a Copilot CLI `--allow-tool` example.
Docs define precedence: `--deny-tool` wins over `--allow-tool`.

questions.stem:
An agent works on the same task from an IDE, from the CLI, and in a GitHub-hosted environment.

For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

items.statement: Referring to the pull request number, the branch name, and commit SHAs allows each tool to retrieve the same state without transferring session context.
items.explanation: These are durable references. Every environment can resolve them against the same repository data.

items.statement: A pull request branch that is behind its base branch is a source of stale context.
items.explanation: The work is based on code that is no longer current, so earlier results may no longer be valid.

items.statement: Restating the acceptance criteria in the prompt of each tool prevents conflicting context.
items.explanation: Copies are what cause conflicting context. Keep the criteria in the issue or pull request and update them there.

questions.explanation: Continuity across tools comes from durable references and a single source of truth, not from copying context. Conflicting context is the same information in several places with different values. Stale context is outdated information used during execution.
questions.takeaway: Share references, not copies. One source per type of information.

evidence.quote: Agent state should be shared using durable references, not copied context.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M5, unit 4

evidence.quote: Don't redefine acceptance criteria in multiple prompts
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M5, unit 4

evidence.quote: A pull request is outdated compared to the base branch
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M5, unit 4

whyExam.skill: Prevent stale context

clues.text: Share state, prevent conflicting context, prevent stale context: three named bullets, one per statement.
M5 unit 4: "Agent state should be shared using durable references, not copied context."

questions.stem:
You are adding repository hooks for GitHub Copilot CLI in `.github/hooks/`.

Which hook should you use for each requirement?

targets.text: Record the result of every tool call for an audit trail.
targets.rationale: `postToolUse` runs after a tool completes, whether it succeeded or failed, so it can log the result.

targets.text: Send an alert when the agent's run fails with an error.
targets.rationale: `errorOccurred` runs when an error occurs during agent execution.

targets.text: Block a shell command that matches a destructive pattern before it runs.
targets.rationale: `preToolUse` runs before the agent uses a tool, and it can approve or deny the execution.

targets.text: Write an audit record when a new agent session begins.
targets.rationale: `sessionStart` runs when a session begins or is resumed.

questions.explanation: A hook runs code at a fixed point of the agent's execution, independently of the model. Only a hook that runs before the tool call can stop it, which makes `preToolUse` the enforcement point. The hooks that run afterwards observe: they log results, report errors and record sessions.
questions.takeaway: Block with `preToolUse`. Log with `postToolUse`. Alert with `errorOccurred`.

evidence.quote: Pre-action hooks Validate or block unsafe actions before execution
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M2, unit 7

evidence.quote: Post-action hooks Log tool usage, outputs, or decisions for auditing
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M2, unit 7

evidence.quote: Error hooks Capture failures and trigger escalation or alerting
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M2, unit 7

evidence.note: Hook events include `sessionStart` (a session begins or is resumed), `preToolUse` (before the agent uses any tool; it can approve or deny tool executions), `postToolUse` (after a tool completes, whether successful or failed) and `errorOccurred` (an error occurs during agent execution). Repository hooks are defined in `.github/hooks/*.json`.
evidence.label: GitHub Docs

questions.stem:
An agent's pull request in a GitHub repository named Repo1 passes all checks and is merged. One week later, an auditor asks which workflow run produced the test report and against which commit. The report was written only to the job log.

You need to make the evidence durable and traceable for future pull requests. Which two actions should you perform? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

options.text: Upload the test report as a workflow artifact.
options.rationale: Correct. An artifact keeps the report as a file that belongs to the run, instead of text inside a log.

options.text: Link the workflow run and its artifacts in an Evidence section of the pull request.
options.rationale: Correct. The link ties the evidence to a specific run, and the run is tied to a specific commit.

options.text: Commit the generated test report to the pull request branch.
options.rationale: Incorrect. Generated files don't belong in the repository. Artifacts keep outputs inspectable without committing them.

options.text: Ask the agent to summarize the test results in a pull request comment.
options.rationale: Incorrect. A summary is the agent's account of the results, not the evidence itself.

options.text: Increase the level of detail of the job log.
options.rationale: Incorrect. More log text doesn't make the report a durable file or link it to the pull request.

questions.explanation: Observability means that every meaningful action leaves an artifact that someone can inspect later. Uploading the report makes it durable, and linking the run and the artifact from the pull request makes it traceable: which run produced it, and against which code state.
questions.takeaway: Upload evidence as artifacts, and link the run from the pull request.

evidence.quote: Uploading artifacts makes evidence durable and reviewable, even when logs scroll away.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M2, unit 7

evidence.quote: Evidence should be traceable to a specific workflow run and a specific commit.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M2, unit 7

evidence.quote: This keeps outputs inspectable and usable without committing generated files back to the repo.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M2, unit 7

whyExam.skill: Configure agent to produce inspectable artifacts within standard development tooling

clues.text: "Minimum observability set" appears twice in M2 u.7 and returns in M4 u.6 and M6 u.6.
Explicit principle: "Evidence should be traceable to a specific workflow run and a specific commit."

questions.stem:
A GitHub organization named Org1 runs an agent workflow that uploads an artifact named `agent-report` on every run. During an incident review, you discover that the artifact is missing from a run that finished two days ago. The repository uses the default retention period for artifacts.

You need to identify who deleted the artifact and when. What should you do?

options.text: Re-run the workflow and compare the new artifact with the job log.
options.rationale: Incorrect. A re-run produces a new artifact. It doesn't show who removed the earlier one.

options.text: Review the timeline of the pull request that triggered the run.
options.rationale: Incorrect. The pull request timeline records commits, reviews and checks. It doesn't record artifact deletions.

options.text: Search the organization audit log for `action:artifact.destroy`.
options.rationale: Correct. The audit log records the manual deletion of a workflow artifact, with the actor, the time and the repository.

options.text: Run `gh agent-task view --log --follow` for the agent session.
options.rationale: Incorrect. That command streams the log of an agent session. It doesn't cover what happened to an artifact afterwards.

questions.explanation: With the default retention period, an artifact from two days ago hasn't expired, so someone deleted it. Deletions of workflow artifacts are written to the organization audit log as `artifact.destroy`, which answers who and when.
questions.takeaway: Missing artifact before it could expire → audit log, `action:artifact.destroy`.

evidence.quote: If workflow artifacts (output files) are unexpectedly missing, GitHub audit logging reveals deletions.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M4, unit 6

evidence.quote: This event shows who deleted an artifact, when, and the affected repository.
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M4, unit 6

evidence.note: The organization audit log lists the event `artifact.destroy`: "A workflow run artifact was manually deleted." By default, artifacts and logs are retained for 90 days.
evidence.label: GitHub Docs

whyExam.skill: Perform post-hoc analysis of multi-agent behavior

clues.text: M4 unit 6 names the exact audit log query `action:artifact.destroy`, a precise, testable fact.
"Post-hoc analysis" is a named bullet.

questions.stem:
You are defining how the work of agents is evaluated in a GitHub repository named Repo1.

For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

items.statement: A passing build proves that an agent's change is complete and low risk.
items.explanation: Checks validate only what they were designed to detect. A passing build says nothing about what isn't tested.

items.statement: Acceptance criteria that are written in the issue give both the agent and the reviewer a basis for verifying completion.
items.explanation: Clear criteria in the issue are the reference for both of them.

items.statement: Selecting a check as a required status check prevents a pull request from being merged until the check passes.
items.explanation: That is what a required status check enforces.

questions.explanation: Evaluation starts from success criteria written in the issue, uses the signals that the pull request shows, and becomes enforceable when checks are required. No single signal is proof of completeness, which is why checks are combined with review.
questions.takeaway: Criteria in the issue, signals in the pull request, enforcement through required checks.

evidence.quote: A passing build does not automatically mean the change is complete, appropriate, or low risk.

evidence.quote: Clear criteria allow both the agent and the reviewer to verify completion.

questions.stem:
Your team plans to increase the autonomy of an agent step by step as the agent proves reliable.

Which four actions should you perform in sequence?

items.text: Allow the agent to open pull requests but not to merge them.
Allow the agent to merge low-risk pull requests after the checks pass.
Allow the agent to deploy to staging automatically.
Allow the agent to deploy to production only through an environment approval.
Allow the agent to push low-risk changes directly to the default branch.
Remove the required status checks for pull requests that the agent opens.

questions.explanation: Progressive autonomy starts with strict controls and relaxes them as the agent earns trust: first proposals only, then merging low-risk changes, then automatic deployment to staging, and production only behind an environment approval. At no stage does the agent get a way around pull requests or checks.
questions.takeaway: Open pull requests → merge low risk → deploy to staging → production with approval.

evidence.quote: Phase 1: agent can only open PRs, can't merge
evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M6, unit 2

evidence.label: Microsoft Learn · M6, unit 2
